legal_basis.from: Reportedly a countywide temporary pause on new AI data centers and battery energy storage systems, suspending county permits, plan reviews, inspections, and related approvals in unincorporated areas, with limited exemptions; no signed July 27 order or minutes were located as of 2026-07-31, only the hearing notice and an unsigned draft order
legal_basis.to: Order of Austin County, Texas, Regarding Battery Energy Storage Systems and Data Centers Health and Safety Review, adopted by the Commissioners Court on 2026-07-27 under Texas Health and Safety Code section 121.003 and Texas Local Government Code section 352.016, among other authorities. The signed, executed order was located directly on austincounty.com (distinct from the earlier unsigned draft). It suspends county permit, plan-review, and inspection approvals for BESS and data center construction in unincorporated areas until a 'Comprehensive Health and Safety Review' (covering fire/life-safety, cybersecurity/foreign-adversary equipment verification tied to the Lone Star Infrastructure Protection Act and the Governor's Prohibited Technologies List, and an Energy Development Zone siting study) is complete, with the Commissioners Court retaining sole discretion over when that review is finished. It requires County Fire Marshal plan review/approval and an independent third-party engineering evaluation before construction, and authorizes the County's legal counsel to seek injunctive relief against violators.
legal_basis.reason: The signed order, fetched directly, is the primary legal-basis text and materially updates and confirms the packet's prior 'reportedly' description; it carries no separate numbered 'Order No.' (Texas county orders of this kind are typically titled descriptively rather than sequentially numbered), which is noted in verify_resolutions.

No repeal, rescission, or completion of the review was found in sources reviewed through 2026-09-23. KWHI notes Austin County is 'the second county in Texas to adopt a moratorium of this nature,' after Hill County (which later rescinded its moratorium following a developer lawsuit; see the existing tx-hill-county-2026 row).

new_candidates.date_enacted: Not yet adopted as of 2026-09-23. On 2026-08-11 the City Council voted (nearly unanimous, with one abstention/one dissent on related items) to begin the legal process toward a 90-day data center moratorium, alongside creating an 11-member Data Center & Infrastructure Commission (chaired by TCU professor Michael Slattery) and requiring state regulatory approval (per Gov. Abbott's directive) before city permits. Per the timeline city staff presented, two public hearings on the moratorium and two additional ordinance-reading hearings are still required; a Data Center & Infrastructure Commission report is due at a Nov. 3, 2026 work session.
new_candidates.duration: Proposed 90 days, extendable once by an additional 90 days (to a 180-day maximum); per the city's own timeline as of August 2026, the moratorium itself would not take effect until approximately Feb. 16, 2027 (running to approximately May 17, 2027, extendable to Aug. 15, 2027), after which state law bars the city from imposing another moratorium for two years.
new_candidates.legal_basis: City Council resolution (Aug. 11, 2026) initiating the statutory process toward a data center moratorium ordinance; not yet a moratorium ordinance itself.
new_candidates.trigger: regulatory_gap and specific_project concerns: sustained public pushback over multiple proposed/under-construction data centers within city limits and the ETJ (e.g., a $10 billion project within 300 feet of a resident's historic garden), a Fort Worth Zoning Commission vote against recommending an initial package of data center zoning regulations (July 2026) as rushed, and a directive from five Council members calling for a moratorium.
new_candidates.current_status: Pending as of 2026-09-23. Fort Worth has not yet adopted a data center moratorium; the Aug. 11, 2026 Council action only began the required legal process (two public hearings plus a two-reading ordinance vote) and created the advisory Data Center & Infrastructure Commission, whose recommendations are due at the council's Nov. 3, 2026 work session. Multiple September 2026 sources (Fort Worth Report, TCU 360, BenbrookLife.com) confirm the moratorium 'is not in place yet.' If the Council ultimately approves it by supermajority following the remaining hearings, city staff's own August 2026 timeline projected the pause would run from approximately Feb. 16, 2027 to May 17, 2027 (extendable to Aug. 15, 2027).
new_candidates.affected_projects: Four data centers operational in Fort Worth as of August 2026, one under construction, four more proposed within city limits, and two proposed in the city's extraterritorial jurisdiction; a $10 billion Edged Data Center project in southwest Fort Worth has drawn particular community opposition (cited by the 2871 Community Coalition advocacy group).
new_candidates.outcome: Council initiated the legal process toward a 90-day (extendable to 180-day) data center moratorium and created an advisory commission; the moratorium itself, if ultimately adopted, would not take effect until roughly Feb. 2027 per the city's own timeline.

evidence.title: Fort Worth sets sights on data center moratorium
evidence.supports: Detailed account of the Aug. 11, 2026 Council action (three measures, near-unanimous votes), the required remaining hearings, and city staff's projected timeline for when a moratorium (if adopted) would actually begin and end.
evidence.quote: If the council approves the moratorium by supermajority, it could begin in February and end in May with the option to extend it for an additional 90 days into August. ... The initial 90-day moratorium would end on May 17, with an option to extend it until Aug. 15.

evidence.quote: This comes after Fort Worth City Council formed and voted for the commission Aug. 11, the same meeting in which they voted to begin the process of a data center moratorium. ... The group is also expected to deliver a report of recommendations to the council by their Nov. 3 work session.

new_candidates.notes: A secondary outlet (Courier Texas, 'Fort Worth unanimously passes data center moratorium') describes the Aug. 11 action in more definitive language than the other three independent sources support; treated here as loose phrasing for the same Aug. 11 resolution-to-begin-the-process, not a separately adopted ordinance, since Fort Worth Report, TCU 360, and BenbrookLife.com all describe the moratorium as not yet in effect as of September 2026.

new_candidates.date_enacted: Not yet adopted as of 2026-09-23. City Council gave staff direction on a Tuesday (per dentonrc.com, a 4-3 vote) to proceed with a possible moratorium and stricter development-code amendments; held the first of two required public hearings on 2026-09-22 (no vote taken); a second public hearing is scheduled for 2026-10-27, with final Council consideration possible as early as 2026-12-02.

new_candidates.legal_basis: Not yet adopted; a proposed ordinance following a two-track process (moratorium plus separate development-code amendments) is pending Council hearings.
new_candidates.trigger: grid_energy/infrastructure_capacity: Denton Municipal Electric's transmission system is reported to be operating near capacity, with roughly $300 million in proposed transmission upgrades awaiting an ERCOT response; residents also cited water and community-benefit concerns relative to the roughly $3.5 million in taxes and $9 million in electric ROI/franchise fees existing data centers generate.
new_candidates.current_status: Pending as of 2026-09-23. The Council held the first of two required public hearings on 2026-09-22, at which all 20 public speakers supported the moratorium (some wanting it stronger); no vote was taken. A second public hearing is scheduled for 2026-10-27, and city officials have outlined a process that could bring the proposal back for final Council consideration as early as 2026-12-02. If adopted, the proposed moratorium would temporarily halt the city's acceptance, processing, and approval of new data center development applications (not affecting already-approved projects).
new_candidates.affected_projects: Not specific to a single named project; framed around the cumulative strain of existing and proposed data centers on Denton Municipal Electric's transmission capacity.
new_candidates.outcome: Two-track process pending: a possible temporary (about 3-month) moratorium and separate, permanent development-code amendments; first of two required public hearings held 2026-09-22, second scheduled 2026-10-27, possible final vote as early as 2026-12-02.

new_candidates.date_enacted: 2026-09-23, Lubbock City Council, 5-2 vote (District 6 Councilman Tim Collins and District 4 Councilman Tim Green dissenting), adopting a resolution to begin the process toward a possible 90-day moratorium.
new_candidates.duration: Proposed 90 days, with a possible optional 90-day extension (would push consideration of a large-scale data center to June 2027 if extended); an 18-month moratorium originally proposed by the citizen 'Save Lubbock' group was deemed not feasible under Texas law.
new_candidates.legal_basis: City Council resolution (2026-09-23) initiating the process toward a data center moratorium ordinance, prompted by a citizen petition from the 'Save Lubbock' group; not yet a moratorium ordinance itself.
new_candidates.trigger: regulatory_gap and specific_project concerns, driven by a citizen petition ('Save Lubbock' group led by Stephen Sanders); Council members cited ERCOT grid conditions and a desire to await further state-level guidance/regulation before large-scale data center development proceeds.
new_candidates.current_status: Pending as of 2026-09-23 (adopted same day as this research date). The Council voted 5-2 to adopt a resolution starting the moratorium process; while the ordinance is drafted, city planning staff are directed to develop guidelines on water use, power reliability, zoning, noise, and lighting for large-scale data centers, and a work session for the Council to be briefed on impacts is to be scheduled within 90 days. No moratorium ordinance has yet been adopted; per Mayor Mark McBrayer, the near-term practical effect is limited since 'no one's coming to Lubbock in the next year anyway with a data center' given current ERCOT conditions.
new_candidates.affected_projects: None named as currently pending before the city.
new_candidates.outcome: Resolution adopted to begin the legal process toward a possible 90-day (optionally extendable to 180-day) data center moratorium, following a citizen petition campaign; the moratorium ordinance itself has not yet been adopted.

evidence.title: City council adopts resolution regarding large-scale data centers in Lubbock, starting process for potential moratorium
evidence.supports: Confirms the 5-2 vote, the dissenting councilmembers' reasoning, the citizen petition origin, the 90-day proposal (with optional 90-day extension), and that this is a resolution starting the process rather than an adopted moratorium.
evidence.quote: The resolution to start the moratorium process was approved 5-2. ... If the optional 90-day moratorium extension were to be approved by council, a potential large-scale data center would not be considered until June of 2027.
